sampling_model.design: Two-arm randomized assignment identifies \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\); the cross-world coupling remains unrestricted.
sampling_model.units: Independent units with ordinal potential outcomes in \(X\), with arm sizes \(n_0\) and \(n_1\).
sampling_model.treatment: Binary randomized treatment \(Z\in\{0,1\}\) with positive assignment probabilities.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Empirical multinomial marginals and simultaneous coordinatewise confidence polytopes \(C_0\) and \(C_1\); no cross-world dependence nuisance is estimated.

body.tldr: Randomization identifies the two ordinal potential-outcome marginals but not their coupling. The proposal characterizes every shortest coupling-robust individual-effect set as a high-mass difference set, gives an exact boundary-safe ternary disconnectedness frontier, and proves that restricting reports to intervals has sharp multiplicative cost \((2L-1)/3\) and additive cost \(2L-4\). Exact min-cut computation and simultaneous multinomial confidence-polytopes provide finite-sample certification and uniform selector recovery away from explicit tie surfaces.

project_justification.gap: The closest ITE papers give sharp distributional bounds and optimize interval-valued reports, but no located result solves the outer cardinality optimization over arbitrary ordinal effect sets; Hall theory certifies a fixed support but does not solve that selection problem.
project_justification.niche: Ordinal outcomes create integer difference geometry in which disconnected sets can be dramatically shorter while remaining valid under every cross-world coupling.
project_justification.fill: The difference-set normal form, complete ternary frontier, sharp general-support interval price, and confidence-polytope inversion jointly deliver identification, geometry, computation, and honest reporting.

body.related_work: Zhang and Richardson (2025), Sections 3 and 5, study coupling-robust ITE prediction intervals; Appendix D and their Theorem 12 establish sharp ordinal individual-effect probability-mass bounds. The sharp interval-price theorem supplies a strict enlargement from their interval oracle to arbitrary effect sets, without attributing an explicit open problem to that paper. Fan and Park (2010) are the direct sharp distribution-of-ITE comparator: they derive Makarov-type distribution-function bounds and inference, whereas the present target selects a shortest common-coupling set of effect values and characterizes when that set is disconnected. Koperberg (2024) supplies finite Strassen--Hall deficiency for a fixed relation and is used only as identification machinery. Lu, Ding, and Dasgupta (2018) derive sharp scalar ordinal benefit bounds through cumulative transportation arguments; the present target is a common-coupling multi-diagonal set. Gao, Shan, Srinivas, and Vijayaraghavan (2025) motivate measuring the exact price of geometric restrictions, but their structured conformal sets are evaluated under an observed outcome law rather than an adversarial potential-outcome coupling. Malloy, Tripathy, and Nowak (2021) motivate simplex confidence-region inversion, Huang, Fang, Hanley, and Rosenblum (2019) address nonregular scalar ordinal-bound inference, and Fang and Santos (2019) explain why active-set ties require directional methods. Duarte and coauthors (2024) motivate exhaustive discrete computation but do not replace the symbolic frontier. Goldman and coauthors (2020) supply the seven-category randomized endpoint for the concrete application.
body.honest_scope: The Hall identity is established prior machinery specialized to this problem. The proposed novelty is the optimizer-wide difference-set geometry, exhaustive ternary frontier, and sharp interval price; all remain to be proved despite the completed finite checks. The confidence result is finite-sample honest but makes no efficiency claim. Selector recovery is asserted only on \(\mathcal M_{L,\eta}\); exact recovery on tie surfaces is not claimed. The irredundant general-\(L\) equality classification remains the open-ended question. When \(L=2\), the reduction agrees with Zhang and Richardson's result that the sole disconnected candidate cannot be shortest, providing the required binary sanity check.
